messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Babies): Babies, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Vignette:
Mateo was 26, a European American fisherman who lived with his wife near the harbor and had built his days around early launches, cold weather gear, and the steady routines of the water. Before the trauma, he had been the sort of man who moved through cramped docks and crowded diners without much thought. That changed after he was taken during a period of political violence overseas and held by men who interrogated, beat, and tortured him over a stretch of days that he still struggled to place in sequence. What remained clearest was not a full story but fragments: a hard room with no place to sit without feeling exposed, the sharp awareness of being pinned in positions that left his body helpless, and the certainty that he could not see who was coming or what they might use next. He had come home with the sense that his body had not entirely left that room.

In the months after returning to the United States, Mateo found that certain ordinary moments brought the event back with sudden force. The cry of babies was one of the fastest ways to unsettle him. When he heard an infant wail in a grocery store aisle or from a stroller on the sidewalk near the marina, his attention snapped hard toward the sound, not because he thought the child itself was dangerous, but because the pitch and urgency seemed to tear open the memory of the interrogation room and the helplessness he had felt there. Bus rides were similarly difficult. He avoided public transport when he could, and when he could not, he sat tensely, tracking the door, the driver, and the other passengers rather than settling into the ride. Being on a bus put him in a seat surrounded by strangers with little room to move, and that position left him feeling exposed in a way he found hard to tolerate. He also noticed how quickly he became uneasy when he felt emotionally vulnerable, especially in moments with his wife when he was expected to talk about what had happened or when he sensed himself becoming tearful. Those moments made him feel unprotected, as if being open in any way left him at risk.

At home, Mateo lived as though danger might enter at any time. He found himself listening for sounds that might mean someone was coming in, particularly at night, and he would go still if he heard the faintest noise near the door or along the hallway. He checked and rechecked whether he could see the room, and he felt safest when his back was against a wall and he could survey everyone else. In restaurants, waiting rooms, and even at church suppers, he took the chair that let him watch the entrance. He also scanned each environment for possible weapons or dangerous objects without always meaning to; he would notice a knife on a counter, a metal tool on the dock, or a broken bottle in a parking lot and feel an immediate tightening in his chest. This habit had become so automatic that his wife noticed he was rarely fully present during meals or family visits, because he was continually orienting himself toward exits, walls, and anything that could be used against him.

When the memories came, they did not arrive as calm recollections. Mateo described feeling intense rage when he remembered what had been done to him, a rage that shocked him because it came so quickly and with so little warning. At times, a flash of memory would bring not only the image but the bodily position back with it: he would tense and fold in on himself as if his body were again arranged the way it had been during the torture, trapped and braced against restraint. He also felt the memory physically in the same parts of his body that had hurt then, as if the pain had been stored there and could be reawakened intact. He did not describe this in poetic terms; he said it in a matter-of-fact way, as though naming an unpleasant fact of his body. The result was that his days had become organized around keeping such moments from breaking in on him.

Over time, these patterns affected the way he moved through both work and home. As a fisherman, Mateo still went out on the boat, but he became increasingly uneasy in enclosed or crowded settings on land, especially during the bus transfers he sometimes needed when work took him away from the dock. At home, his wife began to notice how often he positioned himself with a wall behind him and how frequently he paused to listen before going to bed. He had not sought help at first because he believed he should be able to handle it alone and because naming what had happened felt dangerous in itself. More recently, though, he had become worried that he was living on constant alert and that even his closeness with his wife was being narrowed by his discomfort with feeling exposed. He came for help because he wanted relief from the way babies, buses, and moments of vulnerability could still drop him back into the event, and because he was afraid that if this continued, his life would keep shrinking around the places where he could control what was behind him, what was entering, and what might be used to hurt him again.
